Según Papa Wemba su melodía es centroafricana, de Zaire: viajó con la trata de esclavos a Cuba y de allí a España. La aportación más flamenca fue la de Pepe de la Matrona, que vivió en Cuba a mediados de la década de 1910 (Recuerdos de La Habana, 1914). La rumba catalana tiene su estilo propio, con el Pescaílla, marido de Lola Flores, y Peret, y su toque rapidísimo «del ventilador». Poco apreciada por los flamencos, ha crecido con la salsa entre el público joven; Paco de Lucía tuvo su primer gran éxito con la rumba «Entre dos aguas» y la «Macarena» de Los del Río batió todos los récords. Su baile es sensual y provocador.

scenes.name: La escuela gaditana
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Los cantaores de Cádiz, herederos del Mellizo, dueños de las cantiñas, los tanguillos y las alegrías. Aurelio Sellés (1887-1974) fue uno de sus puntales y dominó cantiñas, siguiriyas, soleares y malagueñas. Pericón de Cádiz (1901-1980) contó su vida en Las mil y una historias de Pericón. La Perla de Cádiz (1925-1975) recreó los estilos de su tierra. Chano Lobato (1927) es el «dueño del compás»: acompañó a Antonio, Matilde Coral y Manuela Vargas y desde los ochenta canta como solista. Les siguen Rancapino, continuador de Aurelio; Chaquetón, de la saga de los Chaqueta y en la línea del Mellizo; Mariana Cornejo, popular por un anuncio cantado por tanguillos; y Juanito Villar, salido de las comparsas de carnaval, que grabó con Paco Cepero.

scenes.name: Villancicos y zambombas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes navideños sobre el nacimiento del «Niño Manuel», de remoto origen profano (hay quien los deriva del zéjel árabe), que el legendario Niño Gloria de Jerez adaptó al compás de bulerías, tangos y tanguillos; sus villancicos los conocen todos los artistas. José Mercé los recreó con gran jondura en la serie Así canta nuestra tierra por Navidad (doce volúmenes), con el tocaor Parrilla de Jerez y el aula de folclore de la Cátedra de Flamencología. En Jerez se celebran por Navidad las zambombas: reuniones familiares en patios de vecinos o bodegas donde se canta en corro por bulerías y tangos, se baila en el centro y se comen pestiños.

scenes.name: Las bulerías
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: El cante festero por excelencia, con el compás de la soleá mucho más acelerado; nacido a comienzos del siglo XX (Mairena atribuye al Loco Mateo, en el XIX, el remate acelerado de las soleares). Tiene dos centros: Cádiz, más larga y suave, y Jerez, más corta y bulliciosa, «la ciudad de los gitanos» de Lorca, donde hasta las piedras cantan por bulerías y el soniquete se lleva en la sangre. El nombre se discute: burla, bolero o bulla. Su métrica lo admite todo, coplas de soleá, seguidillas o canciones (en Utrera, letras de canciones ajenas): un buen cantaor podría cantar por bulerías la guía telefónica. Cierra cualquier festival en el fin de fiesta, y quien la domina en el cante, el baile o el toque domina todo el flamenco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de ida y vuelta: colombiana, guajira, vidalita, milonga
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes folclóricos hispanoamericanos (rumba, milonga, colombiana, guajira, vidalita) aflamencados por la manera de cantarlos en Andalucía; fáciles de cantar, no se consideran cante jondo. Llegaron en la última década del XIX y se difundieron desde los años treinta: son la última gran incorporación al flamenco. La idea de que eran cantes andaluces que fueron a América y volvieron es pura mitopoética. Sabicas contaba que él y Vicente Escudero, con muchos contratos en América y el repertorio flamenco agotado, empezaron a tocar esas canciones «con este aire nuestro». La colombiana no viene de América: la creó Pepe Marchena en los treinta, con enorme éxito; Carmen Amaya fue la primera en cantarla y bailarla, Sabicas la tocaba sin nombrarla por vergüenza y Juanito Valderrama popularizó la suya en los cincuenta. La guajira, de Cuba, fue la primera en llegar y la que mejor se adaptó (en Cádiz se cantaban «guajiras festeras» por bulerías); sus coplas son décimas. La vidalita, del norte argentino y triste, la recuperaron en los noventa jóvenes como Mayte Martín; la milonga pampeana la trajo Pepa Oro en compás de tangos, Chacón la remataba por tanguillos y Pepe de la Matrona la grabó. Hay dos discos fundamentales: Cantes de ida y vuelta (Junta de Andalucía, 1985, con Menese, José Mercé y Luis de Córdoba) y Dos mundos cantan (Expo 92, con Valderrama, Rocío Jurado y Chano Lobato).

scenes.name: Las saetas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cante dolido que solo se canta en Semana Santa, al paso de las imágenes, a palo seco o con cornetas y tambores, por martinetes, siguiriyas (las más comunes), soleares, cañas o polos, con coplas de exaltación religiosa que exigen gran potencia de voz. Nace a finales del XIX en Cádiz: Enrique el Mellizo y sus hijos detenían al Nazareno desde los cuatro balcones de su casa con sus saetas. A él se atribuye la saeta por siguiriyas, que desarrolló Manuel Centeno en el siglo XX. Manuel Torre, el Niño Gloria, la Niña de los Peines, Manolo Caracol y Antonio Mairena eran esperados en Semana Santa para cantarlas sin amplificación desde un balcón a la altura de las imágenes; Manuel Mairena grabó un vía crucis entero. Un equipo francés grabó en directo a los saeteros de Jerez, Arcos y Lebrija en la Semana Santa de 1993 para la colección Flamenco vivo.

scenes.name: Demófilo y los Machado
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Antonio Machado y Álvarez, Demófilo, fue el primer autor español que dedicó un libro entero al flamenco: la Colección de cantes flamencos recogidos y anotados (1881), piedra angular de la flamencología moderna; escribió también sobre las saetas y dirigió la revista El Folclore Andaluz (1882-1883). Sus hijos, los poetas Antonio y Manuel Machado (autor de Cante hondo), heredaron la afición, y sus coplas se cantan a menudo sin que los cantaores sepan que son versos cultos. Calixto Sánchez dedicó a Antonio Machado un disco en 2001, y José Menese hizo suyas las letras de Francisco Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: La farruca y el garrotín
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes aflamencados de fuera de Andalucía. La farruca, gallega, llegó a Cádiz con los comerciantes gallegos del XIX y es más baile que cante; la popularizó Manuel Torre a principios del XX y hoy casi solo la canta Pepe Menese, con una letra de Moreno Galván que se hizo himno en la Transición. Su baile, viril, lo creó Faíco; Carmen Amaya lo bailó vestida de hombre, Falla lo incluyó en El sombrero de tres picos y la versión de Antonio Gades en la película de Los Tarantos, la última de Carmen Amaya, se enseña hoy en las academias. El garrotín viene del folclore asturiano y lo hicieron suyo los gitanos de Lleida; lo difundieron Carmen Amaya y la Niña de los Peines, que lo cantaba con aire de tangos, Faíco hizo sus coreografías y Blas Vega recogió una copla antigua cantada por el Chaparro en la Magna antología del cante flamenco.

scenes.name: Los fandangos de Huelva
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Huelva reclama la cuna del fandango andaluz y es la provincia con más estilos: las antologías recogen más de treinta y cinco, locales (Encinasola, el Alosno, Cabezas Rubias, Calañas, el Andévalo, Valverde del Camino) y personales, creados por profesionales como Paco Isidro, Pepe Rebollo, el Comía, Antonio Rengel, Pérez de Guzmán y Paco Toronjo; de fuera dejaron su sello el Gloria, Macandé, el Carbonerillo y Manolo Caracol. Paco Toronjo, fijo en los festivales desde finales de los sesenta y en las bienales de Sevilla, les dio una jondura difícil de imitar. El baile, de pareja y galanteo, se ve ya poco.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Levante o de las minas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacidos del trabajo en las minas del siglo XIX en las sierras de Cartagena y La Unión y en Linares, La Carolina y Andújar: cantes de dolor profundo sobre la mina, sus accidentes y los compañeros muertos, hechos con fandangos regionales, murcianas, malagueñas y el cante de madrugá de los mineros. La taranta, el más significativo, tiene dos estilos, el de Linares (Gabriel Moreno, Carmen Linares) y el de La Unión (Encarnación Fernández, Pepe Cros), y Camarón le puso dulzura; el taranto, almeriense, tiene compás porque nació para el baile de Carmen Amaya en los cuarenta, con el Ciego de la Playa y Pedro el Morato. La cartagenera, de temas más urbanos, la fijó Antonio Chacón a finales del XIX y la cantaron Cayetano Muriel, Manuel Centeno, Manuel Torre y la Niña de los Peines. La minera se atribuye a Rojo el Alpargatero, Antonio Grau Mora, que hacia 1885 abrió en La Unión una posada que acabó en café cantante y oía cantar a los mineros de madrugada: es el gran creador de los cantes mineros. Las granaínas, de Frasquito Yerbabuena y sobre todo Chacón, son un cante casi barroco hoy cargado de vibratos operísticos. Sin minas, los concursos de Linares y La Unión mantienen vivos estos cantes.

scenes.name: Las cantiñas: alegrías, caracoles, mirabrás y romeras
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes alegres de la bahía de Cádiz, en compás de soleá y muy ligados al baile, que arranca majestuoso y va ganando fuerza hasta desplantes electrizantes. Nacen probablemente de la jotilla gaditana, hermanada con la jota aragonesa por la resistencia común contra Napoleón, de ahí las letras sobre la guerra y el mar; la leyenda atribuye su creación a Enrique el Mellizo, que oyó a una muchacha cantar jotas con un ciego. Tomaron identidad en la segunda mitad del XIX. Hay cantiñas del Pinini de Utrera y Lebrija y de Córdoba; la rosa ya no se canta. Las alegrías, al principio baile de mujer sola, se hicieron más lentas a comienzos del XX y empiezan con el «tirititrán» que, según Chano Lobato, inventó Pericón de Cádiz al olvidar la letra; las cantaron el Mellizo, Ignacio Ezpeleta, Aurelio Sellés, Manolo Vargas y Pericón. Los caracoles, de Tío José el Granaíno (picador del Chiclanero), los recreó Chacón y triunfaron en Madrid («la gran calle de Alcalá»). El mirabrás son alegrías largas (José Menese, con letras de Moreno Galván), y las romeras se atribuyen al Granaíno o a una cantaora llamada la Romera. Hoy el gran intérprete es Chano Lobato.

scenes.name: Los tangos, tientos y marianas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Con bulerías y cantiñas, el gran cante festero: letras de vida, amor y muerte con cierta ligereza, ritmo vivo y pegadizo fácil de seguir con palmas, y un baile sensual. Cádiz y Sevilla se disputan su paternidad, pero los hay en toda Andalucía y en Extremadura; Triana tiene el estilo del Titi y Jerez su propio sello. Su origen musical se discute: Mairena los tenía por cante básico gitano; los estudios recientes los llevan a Cuba y las habaneras llegadas a Sevilla y Cádiz en la segunda mitad del XIX; los granadinos defienden una raíz morisca (el disco Granada canta por tangos recoge trece estilos, entre ellos los de la morería). Manuel Ríos Ruiz concluye que no se sabe con certeza. La Niña de los Peines se hizo inmortal con su copla «Péinate tú con mis peines». Del tango nacen los tientos, más pausados y solemnes, que cantaron primero el Mellizo y el Marrurro y se popularizaron a comienzos del XX, y la mariana, que difundió Bernardo el de los Lobitos y hoy casi solo canta Pepe Menese con letras de Moreno Galván.

scenes.name: Las soleares
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: La madre del cante y uno de sus pilares, independiente de cualquier otro ritmo; los cantaores la consideran «el toro bravo del arte jondo». Coplas solemnes y sentenciosas de tres o cuatro octosílabos, unidas por la guitarra, que suelen rematarse por bulerías; muy apropiadas para el baile de mujer. Se desarrolló al sur del Guadalquivir desde los jaleos festivos: la primera mención es de la Andonda en Triana hacia 1840, una cantaora temible contemporánea del Fillo, y tomó su forma actual entre 1875 y 1915. Las mujeres fueron clave en su creación y transmisión (la Andonda, Mercedes la Serneta, Fernanda de Utrera, Carmen Linares). Hay soleares de Triana (la Andonda, Silverio, Fernando el de Triana, la Niña de los Peines, Tomás Pavón, Mairena), de Alcalá, más solemnes (Joaquín el de la Paula, Juan Talega), de Utrera (la Serneta, el Pinini, María Peña, Fernanda), de Cádiz y el Puerto, más jondas (Enrique Butrón, el Mellizo, Paquirri el Guanté), de Jerez, breves y llenas de melismas (Curro Frijones, José Illanda, Juan Mojama, Tío José de Paula, Manuel Torre) y de Córdoba, más pausadas.

scenes.name: Las siguiriyas, livianas y serranas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Una de las expresiones más dramáticas y de los palos más importantes: sin siguiriyas y soleares el flamenco no sería lo que es. Un quejío entero de lamentos que no admite medias tintas («con las siguiriyas no se puede vender la burra»), con coplas trágicas de cuatro versos (6, 6, 10 y 6 sílabas), muchas sobre la muerte de los seres queridos, y falsetas lentas que suenan a campanas a muerto. Lorca la describió como un grito terrible que divide el paisaje en dos; Tía Anica la Piriñaca decía que cuando la cantaba a gusto la boca le sabía a sangre. La cantaban ya el Planeta (la de la Luna, la más antigua conocida) y el Fillo; luego Manuel Torre, Silverio, Paco la Luz, Cagancho, el Nitri, Curro Dulce, el Loco Mateo, el Mellizo, Terremoto de Jerez (que cantó toda la noche por siguiriyas con su madre muerta en brazos) y Juan Talega; hoy el Chocolate y José Menese. Antonio Mairena grabó unas cuarenta y cinco formas: es el siguiriyero más importante. Sus escuelas son Jerez y los Puertos, Cádiz y Triana. En el baile la difundió Vicente Escudero y Pilar López le añadió los palillos. La liviana, cante de campo, caminos y bandoleros, prepara la voz para la serrana, a la que Silverio dio brillo y con la que se remata por siguiriyas.

scenes.name: La caña, el polo y la petenera
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Tres cantes de la familia de la soleá. La caña, con ayes más arrastrados, se sitúa en la serranía de Ronda (un viajero inglés la oyó allí en 1830) o en la voz árabe gaunia, «canción»; la cantaron el Fillo, Tío José el Granaíno, Antonio Chacón, Pepe de la Matrona y Rafael Romero el Gallina, y hoy se usa más para el baile solemne. El polo se cantaba tras la caña, con la misma métrica; el de Tobalo, su supuesto creador, aparece ya en Estébanez Calderón y hoy se usa en la soleá apolá; Enrique Morente grabó el de Chacón. La petenera, melancólica y de origen incierto, se atribuye a una mujer de Paterna de la Ribera, «la perdición de los hombres», o a los sefardíes de los Balcanes; los gitanos la evitaron porque traía mala suerte. La cantaron la Niña de los Peines, Naranjito de Triana, Rafael Romero, Fosforito y hoy Pepe Menese.

scenes.name: Los cantes de Málaga: malagueñas, rondeñas, jaberas y verdiales
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Después de Sevilla y Cádiz, Málaga es la provincia con más variedad de cantes. La malagueña, cante libre, sin medida y sin baile, de rico toque, ha influido en las granaínas y en todos los cantes minero-levantinos. Nació en Álora (las malagueñas perotas) a partir de los fandangos abandolaos, acompañados de bandola; tras los anónimos y los de Cipriano Pitana, Francisco Jiménez y Joaquín Tabaco, Juan Breva le dio identidad propia, y Lorca escribió de su trino. Su esplendor es la segunda mitad del XIX, con el Canario, la Trini, Baldomero Pacheco y Fosforito el Viejo; también firmaron malagueñas el Mellizo, único gitano creador de una (inspirada en el prefacio de la misa), y Chacón. Diego Clavel recogió treinta y una en los noventa. La rondeña, de principios del XIX y de la tierra del Tobalo, es la pieza con que muchos guitarristas abren sus conciertos; la jabera, ruda y difícil, debe su nombre a una vendedora de habas y está casi perdida; los verdiales, de probable raíz morisca, apenas han cambiado y conservan la panda con violín, panderos, chinchines y cañas para la fiesta de san Juan.

scenes.name: Los tanguillos de Cádiz
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Vinculados al carnaval de Cádiz, son el soporte de chirigotas, coros y murgas; cantados en grupo pierden su naturaleza flamenca, que es individual, aunque como baile la conservan. Hay constancia de los «tangos graciosos» del barrio de La Viña en 1779, en la tonadilla La anónima de Tomás Abril, y el tango americano o de negros terminó de formarlos. Letras jocosas y satíricas: «el chiste ingenuo y feliz enfrente de la tragedia jonda del quejío» (Emilio Jiménez Díaz). Aurelio y Pericón de Cádiz, Manuel Vargas y la Perla los grabaron en la primera mitad del siglo XX, y hasta Mairena dejó dos. Chano Lobato, su mayor cultor, los elevó a cante noble y recrea la venta de los cuadros que popularizó Pericón.

scenes.name: Las tonás: martinetes, carceleras y deblas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Cantes sin acompañamiento, prueba de su antigüedad, en cuartetas octosílabas de intensa carga dramática y origen gitano indiscutible: son crónicas de la miseria, la cárcel y la persecución. Demófilo ya las daba en 1881 por «cantes viejos casi caídos en desuso»; en el siglo XIX hubo entre veintisiete y treinta y cuatro, cada una con el nombre de su creador. La más antigua es la de Tío Luis el de la Juliana, aguador y primer cantaor del que hay noticia (segunda mitad del siglo XVIII), conservada por Antonio Chacón y recreada por Pepe de la Matrona; se le atribuye también la toná de los pajaritos, que recuerda la tonada sefardí de los bilbilicos. Los martinetes toman el nombre del martillo de la fragua, aunque es difícil cantar mientras se forja: Tío Juane de Jerez montaba una fragua en escena en los setenta y ochenta, y Antonio el Bailarín creó su baile con martillo y yunque; la familia fragüera más antigua es la de los Cantorales de Cádiz, que Silverio visitaba. Las carceleras cantan la prisión y servían para pasar mensajes en romaní desde las rejas. La debla, único palo con nombre romaní («diosa»), es religiosa, casi perdida y muy difícil; llegó a hoy por Tomás Pavón en los cuarenta y la recuperó Antonio Mairena.

scenes.name: Las sevillanas
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Nacen de las seguidillas castellanas, que en Sevilla se hicieron más vivas y fáciles de repetir: cuatro coplas para bailar en pareja un galanteo, con temas andaluces, amorosos o rocieros (corraleras, rocieras, bíblicas, de feria, marineras, romeras). Lorca recogió una del siglo XVIII. Su gran auge comercial llegó en los setenta, con millones de discos que daban envidia a los flamencos; las han grabado con jondura Manuel Vallejo, la Niña de los Peines, la Paquera de Jerez, el Turronero, Chiquetete y Camarón.

scenes.name: El fandango
scenes.book: El flamenco contado con sencillez
scenes.desc: Muy apreciado por su musicalidad y fácil de interpretar, no es un palo básico pero no es menor: la vieja división entre cantes grandes y chicos está obsoleta, y la jondura la pone el intérprete, no la antigüedad del palo. Canto para bailar de origen muy antiguo e incierto (Corominas lo deriva del portugués fado; hay quien le ve un lejano origen árabe), aparece por escrito en un entremés de 1705 y lo describe el deán Manuel Martí en 1712; en el siglo XIX fue el cante y baile nacional español, y a finales de siglo se aflamencó en Andalucía y dejó de bailarse. De él salen las granaínas, las malagueñas y los cantes de Levante, y hay fandangos propios en Lucena, Cabra, Puente Genil, Jaén, Granada o Almería. Su apogeo en la ópera flamenca lo desprestigió tanto que a cantaores como Pepe Menese les parece un insulto que se lo pidan; desde los años ochenta se revaloriza.

facts.title: "Scary Monsters" Video (1980) - New Romantic Catalyst
facts.body: David Bowie co-directed a groundbreaking video for a song from his "Scary Monsters" album in 1980, which notably used the Quantel Paintbox for special effects. Shot at Beechie Head in East Sussex, the video was a dream sequence featuring Bowie as a clown, an astronaut (referencing Ziggy Stardust and the movie Alien), and a mental patient, with costuming inspired by "The Sound of Music." Extras from London's avant-garde Blitz Club, including Steve Strange (later of Visage), contributed to its distinctive look. Costing $65,000 ($250,000 today), this surreal and fashionable video helped launch the New Romantic movement of the early 1980s. "Bowie's surreal but very fashionable clown character helped jumpstart the whole new romantic movement of the early 1980s."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Major Tom's Return - "Ashes to Ashes" (1980)
facts.body: Bowie revived his beloved character Major Tom in the lead single for "Scary Monsters," portraying him as a "doomed astronaut" aimlessly knocking through space while "strung out on a kind of galactic heroine." This cheeky continuation of the character's story was a key element of the single's UK success. "Maybe that was because on its lead single, Bowie was reviving his most beloved character, Major Tom."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: "Ashes to Ashes" Music Video (1980)
facts.body: The music video for "Ashes to Ashes" was a colorful, high-concept, and very expensive production, reportedly costing a quarter million pounds. It premiered on the BBC's "Top of the Pops" and contributed significantly to the single becoming David Bowie's fastest-selling UK single ever. "Promoted with a colorful, high concept and very expensive music video that premiered on the BBC's Top of the Pops and was reported to have cost a quarter million pounds."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: Starman to Blackstar Edition Part 2
facts.name: David Bowie

facts.title: Soviet State-Sponsored Bootlegging (1980)
facts.body: By 1980, the Soviet state recording company Melodia began bootlegging recordings by The Beatles and The Rolling Stones under Kremlin supervision. This act, while intellectual property theft, inadvertently served the CIA's goal of distributing Western music and soft power to the Soviet population. "By 1980, under supervision from the Kremlin, state recording company Melodia, started bootlegging recordings by the Beatles and the Rolling Stones."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Great KGB Punk Rock Conspiracy

facts.title: Post-1980 Continuation and Commercialization
facts.body: After 1980, punk rock continued its presence, but it gradually became significantly dominated and influenced by multinational corporations. This marked a shift from its earlier independent origins, as it persisted as a stylistic remnant during the highly effervescent early 1980s musical landscape. "el punk continuó un poco más allá en 1980 pero ya fue dominado bastante por algunas multinacionales."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: El papel de REM en los '80
facts.name: Punk

facts.title: Volatile Recording Sessions with Phil Spector (1980)
facts.body: For their *End of the Century* album, The Ramones worked with legendary producer Phil Spector, known for his "Wall of Sound" but also his perfectionism and violent temper. Spector had pursued the band for years, seeing their "punk melodicism" as a replica of his classic sound. The band agreed to work with him to expand their fanbase but regretted the decision due to Spector locking them in the studio, demanding endless takes, and allegedly holding Joey and Dee Dee Ramone hostage at gunpoint. "A decision the Ramones came to regret when Specter locked them in the studio and made them do take after take."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: The Ramones

facts.title: Dominance Post-1980 Recession
facts.body: After the severe recession of 1980, as the gloom began to lift around 1983-1984, pop music entered a period of dominance. "But once the gloom of that began to lift around 1983, 84, what do we get? A period where pop music dominated."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Major Label Adoption (By 1980)
facts.body: Seymour Stein's "New Wave" marketing term was swiftly embraced by major labels, including Warner Brothers Records and Polygram Records. By 1980, this led to "New Wave" becoming a widely used catch-all term for a broad spectrum of experimental, artsy, and more poppy music that emerged in the wake of punk. "Seymour's marketing term was then picked up by Warner Brothers Records, and then by Polygram Records, and then other major labels."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Etymology: Part 1
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: Times Square Soundtrack Introduction (1980)
facts.body: The soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square* was one of the very first to feature the nascent new wave and punk rock music of the day. Despite the movie and double LP's dismal sales, for those who purchased it, it offered an immediate look at cutting-edge music and significantly contributed to introducing people to these genres. "Time Square did a lot to introduce people to punk a new wave."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks
facts.name: New Wave

facts.title: Strong Presence in New York (1980)
facts.body: New Wave was a very potent musical force in New York around 1980, exemplified by bands like Devo. "El New Wave en Nueva York. Allá en 1908 entra a muy potente, gracias adivo, entre otras bandas."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan

facts.title: Ian Curtis's Suicide (1980)
facts.body: Singer Ian Curtis killed himself on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and substance abuse problems related to his illnesses, and had attempted suicide at least once before. His deteriorating condition was compounded by marital problems. The day before the band's first North American tour, Ian stayed up all night watching TV, listening to music, drinking whiskey and coffee, then hanged himself in his kitchen with a clothesline. His wife, Deborah, found him the next morning. "Ian had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and all manner of substance abuse problems related to his illnesses."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Groups That Changed Their Front-Person and Survived
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Ian Curtis's Struggles (Spring 1980)
facts.body: By spring 1980, Ian Curtis was battling drugs and alcohol, having an affair, and contemplating divorcing his wife. He suffered from severe epilepsy, with seizures becoming more frequent and medication having little effect. Despite the band's rising success and a booked American tour, Curtis was terribly depressed and considering quitting the band to open a bookshop on the continent. "Singer Ian Curtis was battling drugs in alcohol. He was having an affair with a Belgian woman while his wife went to work and cared for their baby daughter. And Ian had a severe case of epilepsy which seemed to be getting worse and worse."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Final Concert and Seizure (May 2, 1980)
facts.body: Joy Division's last concert was held at Birmingham University on May 2, 1980, and was recorded. During the performance of "Decades," Ian Curtis fainted on stage due to an epileptic seizure. The audience initially mistook his collapse for an intense dance move and cheered. Curtis was helped off stage, recovered, and returned for an encore, marking his final stage appearance. He died by suicide less than two weeks later. "The final joy division gig was held on May 2nd, 1980 at Birmingham University. The show was recorded."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Legendary Gigs
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Through Two Albums and Ian Curtis's Suicide (Until May 1980)
facts.body: Rob Gretton was the dedicated manager for Joy Division throughout the release of their two albums. His tenure with the band also encompassed the tragic event of singer Ian Curtis's suicide in May 1980.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Mighty Managers of Rock
facts.name: Joy Division

facts.title: Depression and Personal Turmoil (April 1980)
facts.body: By April 1980, Ian Curtis was severely depressed, a state compounded not only by his epilepsy but also by a failing affair with a Belgian fan, the impending split from his wife, and dire financial difficulties that forced them to give away their family dog. He desired solitude but was ill-equipped to live alone. "By April 1980, Ian was very, very depressed. Not just as a result of the epilepsy either. He was having an affair with a Belgian fan. facts.title: Suicide (May 18, 1980)
facts.body: After previous suicide attempts, Ian Curtis took his own life by hanging himself from a clothesline in his kitchen in the early morning hours of May 18, 1980. This tragic event occurred on the very day Joy Division was scheduled to depart for their first-ever tour of North America. "There had been some suicide attempts. By the early morning hours of May 18, 1980, Ian couldn't take it anymore. He hanged himself from the clothesline in the kitchen of his house. That Monday was the day joy division was supposed to leave for their first ever tour of North America."

facts.title: Final Concert and Seizure (May 2, 1980)
facts.body: Joy Division's last concert was held at Birmingham University on May 2, 1980, and was recorded. During the performance of "Decades," Ian Curtis fainted on stage due to an epileptic seizure. The audience initially mistook his collapse for an intense dance move and cheered. Curtis was helped off stage, recovered, and returned for an encore, marking his final stage appearance. He died by suicide less than two weeks later. "The final joy division gig was held on May 2nd, 1980 at Birmingham University. The show was recorded."

facts.title: Ian Curtis's Struggles (Spring 1980)
facts.body: By spring 1980, Ian Curtis was battling drugs and alcohol, having an affair, and contemplating divorcing his wife. He suffered from severe epilepsy, with seizures becoming more frequent and medication having little effect. Despite the band's rising success and a booked American tour, Curtis was terribly depressed and considering quitting the band to open a bookshop on the continent. "Singer Ian Curtis was battling drugs in alcohol. He was having an affair with a Belgian woman while his wife went to work and cared for their baby daughter. And Ian had a severe case of epilepsy which seemed to be getting worse and worse."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Ian Curtis's Suicide (1980)
facts.body: Singer Ian Curtis killed himself on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and substance abuse problems related to his illnesses, and had attempted suicide at least once before. His deteriorating condition was compounded by marital problems. The day before the band's first North American tour, Ian stayed up all night watching TV, listening to music, drinking whiskey and coffee, then hanged himself in his kitchen with a clothesline. His wife, Deborah, found him the next morning. "Ian had been suffering from severe depression, epilepsy, and all manner of substance abuse problems related to his illnesses."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Early Deal with Mute Records (1980)
facts.body: In the fall of 1980, Depeche Mode was one of the first bands to sign with Mute Records, an all-synthesizer-based label. Their verbal agreement stipulated a 50/50 split of proceeds from domestic releases and a 70/30 split (band/label) for international sales, a handshake deal that remained unwritten until 1986 due to strong trust. "They were one of the first people to sign into a new all synthesizer base label called mute in the fall of 1980. They struck a deal whereby all proceeds from the domestic releases would be split 50 50 with the label and the money from international sales would be split 70 30."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 25 Random Facts About Depeche Mode
facts.name: Depeche Mode

facts.title: "Pornography of Pop" Criticism (1980)
facts.body: In 1980, Eric Siegel penned a scathing article for the Baltimore Sun titled "Heavy Metal is the Porno of Pop," claiming the genre possessed "no redeeming social value." Siegel criticized heavy metal bands like Van Halen, Judas Priest, and Ted Nugent for sounding identical, lacking originality, and being misogynistic. "heavy metal stands as the hardcore pornography of popular music. No redeeming social value."

facts.title: Economic Downturn Contribution (1980)
facts.body: The bursting of the disco bubble in 1980 contributed to a major recession in the recording industry, with sales dropping 10% year over year. This economic downturn, coupled with high interest rates, meant that people were less willing to spend discretionary income, making the industry ripe for a new marketing tool like music videos. "The disco bubble had burst."

facts.body: Film director John Landis was reportedly surprised when Franklin accepted a small acting cameo as a waitress in his 1980 musical film *The Blues Brothers*, remarking that "she didn't have anything else going on." Her performance of "Think" in the film provided much-needed positive exposure after her disco struggles. "When film director John Landis invited her to do a small acting cameo as a waitress in his 1980 musical film The Blues Brothers, he was almost shocked when she said yes, quote, she didn't have anything else going on, he later said."

facts.title: First Gig and Origin (1980)
facts.body: R.E.M. played their inaugural gig on Saturday, April 5, 1980, at Kathleen O'Brien's 20th birthday party. The event was held in a former Episcopalian church on Oakley Street that had been repurposed as a "flop house" for University of Georgia students. The four band members, using borrowed instruments, performed primarily for free beer and initially had no plans to continue as a group.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Career Launch Triggered by Theft (1980)
facts.body: The band's unexpected career trajectory began when a frat boy stole a fancy and expensive Budweiser beer tap from the party, which Kathleen O'Brien had rented with a bad check deposit. Feeling bad for Kathleen, the band decided to play an additional gig at a local club to raise money for the stolen tap. This second performance led to more shows, and soon, R.E.M. became a full-time concern, all stemming from the theft.
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 9
facts.name: R.E.M.

facts.title: Formation and Early Reception (1980)
facts.body: R.E.M. emerged in 1980 during a period of immense musical ferment, when various genres like punk, electronic pop, and hip hop were evolving, and guitar sounds were becoming increasingly hard and distorted. Initially, the band struggled to gain interest from major labels, spending years sending out demos and performing frequent local university concerts where they cultivated a dedicated fanbase. facts.body: The soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square* was notable for being one of the very first to feature the nascent alternative music of the day, specifically punk rock and new wave. Despite its commercial failure, it offered an early glimpse into cutting-edge music for those who acquired it. "The soundtrack is notable in that it was one of the very first to feature the nascent alternative music of the day."

facts.title: North American Term Origin (1980)
facts.body: The term "alternative" in North America dates back to at least 1980, emerging as rock began to fragment. It originally described music from artists rejected by major labels due to smaller audiences, finding homes with small regional labels like Berserkli and Rounder. These labels and their music were seen as an "alternative" to the mainstream. "Now alternative dates back to at least 1980, a time when rock was really starting to fragment."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

facts.title: Xanadu Movie Flop (1980)
facts.body: Olivia Newton-John considered agreeing to star in *Xanadu* a mistake, as she signed on based on an 18-page treatment with no script. The script was then continuously written and rewritten during filming, contributing to the movie's commercial failure, despite its well-received soundtrack. "Olivia said that her mistake was agreeing to it because she liked the idea that there was no script and so she disagreed to it based on an 18-page treatment and then it was written and rewritten while it was being shot."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s

facts.title: Transition to New Wave Era (1980)
facts.body: At the start of the 1980s, Blondie was among several bands attempting to expand the definition of punk to achieve pop chart success. Their single "Atomic" in early 1980 was key in pointing a way forward for them in the new wave era, blending surf rock, cowboy twang, and danceable rock elements. "What was most important about Atomic was how it pointed away forward for Blondie in the new wave era."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: Blondie

facts.title: Collaborations with Giorgio Moroder (1980)
facts.body: Debbie Harry was invited to contribute to the soundtrack of Paul Schrader's 1980 film *American Gigolo*. The film's score was overseen by Italian producer Giorgio Moroder, known for his work with Donna Summer and his Oscar-winning score for *Midnight Express*. Moroder was seen as an ideal producer to steer Blondie towards electronic music and danceable rock, leading to the creation of "Call Me." "This made Moroder, perhaps the ideal producer to push Blondie further in the direction of electronic music and danceable rock."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia
facts.episode: This Ain’t No Party! Edition Part 2
facts.name: Blondie

facts.title: Debbie Harry's Celebrity Status (1980-1981)
facts.body: During the recording of *Autoamerican*, Debbie Harry's prominence grew significantly. She was invited as a showcase guest on an episode of "The Muppet Show" and Blondie was approached to contribute a theme song for the James Bond film *For Your Eyes Only*. Harry also recorded a solo album during this period, indicating her rising individual stardom. "Debbie Harry was invited to be the showcase guest on an episode of The Muppet Show."
facts.source: Hit Parade Music History and Music Trivia

facts.title: Flash Gordon (1980) - Soundtrack Iconography
facts.body: While the "Flash Gordon" soundtrack album is considered one of Queen's lower artistic moments, its iconography is fantastic. The band masterfully integrated their image with Flash Gordon's superhero iconography, creating numerous intriguing posters. This era produced one of Freddie Mercury's most iconic looks: wearing a Flash Gordon t-shirt, leather shorts, and famously pictured atop a Darth Vader figure. "Nos lejó uno de los momentos icónicos más maravillosos de Freddy Mercury con la camiseta de Flash Gordon, unos y ors de cuero subido encima de Darth Vader."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: QUEEN como iconografía estética y gráfica

facts.title: Death by Suicide (May 18, 1980)
facts.body: Ian Curtis died by suicide on May 18, 1980, at the age of 23. He had been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures exacerbated by a "crazy cocktail" of prescriptions, drinking, illegal drug use, poor diet, and late nights. He also faced an impending divorce, an affair with a Belgian woman, money worries, and pressure to continue performing with Joy Division despite his problems. The final Joy Division show on May 2, 1980, saw Ian faint during the last song, experiencing another grand mal seizure, leading to the cancellation of their upcoming North American tour. On the evening of May 17, Ian returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank strong coffee and whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on May 18, he put on his favorite album, "The Idiot" by Iggy Pop, went to the garden for a length of rope from the clothesline, and hanged himself. Deborah found him a few hours later. "He'd been in very poor health, suffering from epileptic seizures that were exacerbated by a crazy cocktail of prescriptions, drinking illegal drug use, poor diet late nights, an impending divorce, and a ferry was having with a woman from Belgium worries about money and pressures to keep on performing with the band despite all these problems."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Hours Of...
facts.name: Ian Curtis

facts.title: Final Joy Division Performance (May 2, 1980)
facts.body: During what would be Joy Division's final show, Ian Curtis fainted and went into another grand mal seizure during the last song. This incident led to the decision to cancel all upcoming shows before the band was scheduled to leave for their first-ever North American tour, which was planned for two weeks later. "The final joint evision show was held on May 2nd, 1980. During the final song, Ian fainted and went into another grandmaw seizure."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Hours Of...
facts.name: Ian Curtis

facts.title: Pre-Suicide Activities (May 17-18, 1980)
facts.body: On the evening of May 17, 1980, Ian Curtis returned to his home at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester, while his wife Deborah was out. He watched the 1977 film "Strozek," which depicted a musician unable to decide between two women in his life, and consumed several cups of strong coffee and a shot of whiskey. With pictures of his wife and baby daughters in front of him, he spent the entire night writing a long note to Deborah. As the sun came up on May 18, he put on Iggy Pop's album "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from the garden clothesline, and hanged himself. "Once she was gone, Ian sat down to watch his movie, which was a 1977 film entitled Strozek, which follows a musician and formmental patient who travels to the US and is unable to decide between the two women in his life."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Hours Of...
facts.name: Ian Curtis

facts.title: Pre-Suicide Activities (1980)
facts.body: In the days leading up to his death, Ian seemed to be in good spirits, with no seizures reported. On Thursday, May 15th, 1980, he played pool with bassist Peter Hook. The next day, Peter dropped Ian off at his parents' house with instructions to pack for the upcoming American tour. On Saturday, May 17th, Ian bailed on plans to water ski with guitarist Barney Sumner, citing a need to rest and wanting to watch a cool movie on TV. "On Thursday May 15th, 1980, Ian hung out with bass player Peter Hook playing pool in a local pub."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Hours Of...
facts.name: Ian Curtis

facts.title: Final Hours and Suicide (1980)
facts.body: On the evening of May 17th, Ian returned to his house at 77 Barton Street in Macclesfield, Manchester. His wife, Deborah, was working as a bartender at a wedding reception. They spoke, and Ian requested time alone, with Deborah agreeing not to return until after 10 AM the next morning, spending the night at her parents' house. After she left, Ian watched the 1977 film "Strozek," drank several cups of strong coffee and a shot of whiskey, and then wrote a long note to Deborah all night. As the sun rose on Sunday, May 18th, he put on Iggy Pop's "The Idiot," retrieved a rope from his garden's clothesline, and hanged himself. "Once she was gone, Ian sat down to watch his movie, which was a 1977 film entitled Strozek, which follows a musician and form a mental patient who travels to the US and is unable to decide between the two women in his life."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Hours Of...
facts.name: Ian Curtis

facts.body: Ian Curtis's body was found a few hours later by his wife, Deborah. He was 23 years old at the time of his death. "It was Deborah who would find him a few hours later. Ian Curtis, dead by suicide on May 18th, 1980, age 23."

facts.title: Central Park Collapse (September 1980)
facts.body: Before his second show at Madison Square Garden on September 20, 1980, while running with his friend Alan Cole in Central Park, Bob Marley experienced altered vision, difficulty speaking, tightened legs, and searing neck pain, culminating in a multi-minute seizure and collapse. Despite this, he insisted on checking himself out of the hospital to perform the concert that night. "But before the second show, Bob went running with his friend Alan Cole in Central Park. His vision began to alter. He had trouble speaking. Suddenly his legs tightened, and he felt a searing pain in his neck. He collapsed and went into a seizure that lasted for several minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Widespread Cancer and Unsuccessful Treatments (September 1980)
facts.body: After collapsing in Central Park, Bob Marley reported back to the hospital on September 26, 1980, where doctors discovered that the melanoma had spread from his toe to his brain, forming a massive tumor, and also to his liver and lungs. He underwent chemotherapy and radiation treatments at Sloan Kettering Hospital, which caused his dreadlocks to fall out, leading to his wife giving him his first haircut in years. However, these conventional treatments proved ineffective. "doctors reported that the cancer had spread from his toe to his brain. There was a massive tumor. They also found cancer in his liver and lungs." "But the chemo and radiation did not work. There was nothing more they could do."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Experimental Treatments with Dr. Joseph Issels (November 1980 - February 1981)
facts.body: Discharged with only weeks to live, Bob Marley sought alternative treatments in Europe from Dr. Joseph Issels, a controversial figure described as a former Nazi who worked for Josef Mengele but resigned after refusing orders to stop treating Jewish patients. In Bavaria in November 1980, Marley, though weak, underwent Issels' experimental methods, including a special macrobiotic diet and drug-induced fevers using toxins to stimulate the immune system, along with the removal of decaying teeth and tonsils. By February 1981, after his 36th birthday, Issels attempted painful ozone injections into his navel, which only produced epileptic-like seizures and proved unsuccessful. "Through one of his Rastafarian contacts in Jamaica, he'd heard of a doctor named Joseph Isles, a former Nazi apparently, a guy who used to work for Joseph Mangalup." "Isles was offering some experimental cancer treatments."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Last Moments Of - Part 1
facts.name: Bob Marley

facts.title: Cult Status Before Debut Album (Pre-1980)
facts.body: The press initially struggled to categorize The Cramps, and they did not release their first album until 1980. This unique situation contributed to their growth into a significant cult phenomenon within the underground music scene. "La prensa a tardón a hacerles caso ya que eran una banda difícil de englobar y nos sacaron disco hasta 1980, cosa que los convirtió en un fenómeno de culto."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps
facts.name: The Cramps

facts.title: Bryan Gregory's Mid-Tour Departure (1980)
facts.body: Shortly after the release of *Songs the Lord Taught Us* in 1980, guitarist Bryan Gregory abandoned the band mid-tour, reportedly taking the band's van and equipment with him. Rumors circulated that he had joined a satanic cult, but the truth was he was experiencing a crisis exacerbated by heroin use. "Poco después de sacar el disco, Reyangre goria abandonó la banda amplia en la gira, llevándose consigo a la forgoneta y el equipo. Corrió el rumor entre las cena y los fans de que se había unido en la secta satanica. Lo cierto es que estaba pasando por una crisis potenciada por la heroína."
facts.source: Central Sonora
facts.episode: Amor, Terror y Psychobilly: La Historia de The Cramps
facts.name: The Cramps

facts.title: Four Lead Singers – Bon Scott Died 1980, Brian Johnson Made Back in Black, Axl Rose Subbed in 2016
facts.body: AC/DC has had four lead singers. Dave Evans was the original, present from the band's 1973 formation through their glam-rock phase. Bon Scott replaced him after being discovered working as the band's chauffeur; he recorded seven albums cementing AC/DC's reputation but died of acute alcohol poisoning on February 19, 1980. Brian Johnson replaced him in time for *Back in Black* (1980), which has sold at least 50 million copies. When Johnson developed serious ear problems in 2016, Axl Rose of Guns N' Roses sang for approximately two dozen shows; Johnson subsequently received treatment and rejoined. "The swap worked way better than anyone could have dreamed."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 18 Bands Who Changed Lead Singers
facts.name: AC/DC

facts.title: 1980 High Voltage Tour at Kiel Opera House
facts.body: AC/DC's "High Voltage Tour" took place on September 18, 1980, at the Kiel Opera House. The concert was heavily promoted, with tickets available at various outlets including Backstage Records, Lane Co-op, Spectrum, Peaches, the Kiel Opera House box office, and through Dial Tix. "Plug into the 1980 AC DC high voltage tour. E-lectrophying. Scorching AC DC live in concerts of September 18 at the Kiel opera house."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Weird History of Concert Tickets Part 2

facts.title: Evolution of Sound (1980-81)
facts.body: Between 1980 and 1981, Technopop began to change significantly due to advancements in technology, allowing for more diverse sounds, especially dance speeds. Songs became less intense, singing more emotive, and instrumentation thicker, thanks to new polyphonic synthesizers and FM synthesis, moving away from thin, trebly sounds. "However, all this began to change in 1980 and 1981, when the technology advanced to allow for even more sounds, specifically dance speeds."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Post-Punk Explosion Part 2: Techno-Pop
facts.name: Technopop

facts.title: Second Wave (Post-mid 1980) – Joyous and Danceable
facts.body: This later period shifted towards electronic music that was danceable, joyous, and fun, reflecting an atmosphere of returning optimism as economic recession began to dissipate. "And we got into our second wave which features the kind of electronic music you can dance to. Synthesizing music didn't have to be all gloomy and detached. It could also be joyous and fun."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Roots of New Wave through Techno-Pop
facts.name: Technopop

facts.title: David Bowie's Influence (1980)
facts.body: The New Romantic movement of the early 1980s was significantly jumpstarted by David Bowie's surreal yet fashionable clown character in his groundbreaking 1980 music video for a song from his "Scary Monsters" album. This visual style, featuring elements like extras from the Blitz Club, became highly influential. "Bowie's surreal but very fashionable clown character helped jumpstart the whole new romantic movement of the early 1980s."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The Rise and Fall and Future of the Music Video - Part 1
facts.name: New Romantic

facts.title: First Gig – December 8, 1980; John Lennon Shot That Day
facts.body: 54-40 played their first gig on December 8, 1980 in Vancouver — the same day John Lennon was shot. They learned of the shooting on the radio on the way to the show. They performed approximately four original songs on an open mic night, and the timing gave the performance an unexpectedly profound emotional weight. "One of those all quiet on the Western front type of moments where it's like, you know, Johnny's just been shot."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 54-40 In Their Own Words Part 1

facts.title: Vancouver Origins – Fear and Loathing Road Trip Down the Coast, Following Young Canadians (1980)
facts.body: Before forming 54-40 in the fall of 1980, Brad Merritt, Neil Osborne, and Randy (an early member) followed the Young Canadians on a Fear and Loathing–style road trip down the California coast in 1980, visiting venues like the Whisky a Go Go in Los Angeles. Vancouver's punk and alternative scene, including D.O.A. and the Young Canadians, regularly traveled the north-south corridor to Seattle, Portland, and San Francisco. "We felt super fortunate to have been a part of that, to see these bands and be part of that scene."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 54-40 In Their Own Words Part 1

facts.title: Chaotic New York Concert (May 15, 1980)
facts.body: Public Image Limited (P.I.L.), led by Johnny Lydon (formerly Johnny Rotten), agreed to play two nights at the Ritz in New York for a $12,000 fee, despite internal squabbles, drug abuse, and money problems. The band was in no shape to play, lacking a drummer (the sixth one quit) and a bass player (who had just walked out). They quickly hired a 65-year-old jazz drummer from a Broadway music shop. Instead of performing live, P.I.L. pantomimed along to their records, hidden from the audience by a large screen with their silhouettes projected by bright white lights. The 1,500 people in the audience were kept waiting in the pouring rain for over an hour, then discovered the band wasn't playing, and Johnny Lydon began taunting and insulting the crowd. This led to a rain of garbage, a storming of the stage, and the destruction of all equipment, with the gig ending after just 25 minutes. "The gig was killed after just 25 minutes."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: From the Archives: The Top 100 Moments in New Rock - Part 8
facts.name: Public Image Ltd

facts.title: Perspective on Popular Music (1980)
facts.body: In 1980, Billy Joel observed that the fundamental appeal of popular music, including rock and roll, pop, funk, lies initially in its "beat" and "melody," with lyrics being something listeners dig into later if they truly enjoy the song. He applied this to "My Sharona," noting its "pubescent dumbbo words" fit the song's overall appeal. "Rock and roll pop funk. They can all be so many things, both reflective and reactive. But let's remember the essence of popular music. A song comes on. What do you hear first? Words? Nah, you hear a beat. Then a melody."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 34 - A 70s Pop Manifesto - Finding Meaning in 70s Pop
facts.name: Billy Joel

facts.title: Second Studio Album
facts.body: Joy Division began recording their second album, *Closer*, in 1980. For many, this album is not as famous as their debut but is considered to be of higher quality, and some fans even regard it as possibly the best Post-Punk work. "primero en 1980 empiezan la grabación del Closer, lo que sería el segundo disco, para muchos no tan famos como el primero, pero sí que posiblemente va a estar de mejor calidad que el segundo."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 2. Unknown Pleasures
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Second Studio Album
facts.body: Recorded between March 18 and 20, 1980, this album featured a deeper, richer, and more haunting vocal delivery from Ian Curtis, achieved through producer Martin Hannett and Tony Wilson making him listen to Frank Sinatra records. It marked the band's artistic progression and intensified their sound of pain and alienation. "Between March 18 and 20, 1980, they started recording a new album that would eventually be called Closer."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: What's the Big Deal About Joy Division?
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Early 1980 Recording Start
facts.body: The band wasted no time after *Unknown Pleasures*, beginning work on their second album, *Closer*, very early in 1980. "no dejaron casi pasar tiempo hasta que empezaron a trabajar el segundo álbum y tenemos así como el closer empieza a grabarse muy a primeros en 1980."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Recording and Release Timeline
facts.body: The album *Closer* was recorded in March 1980, and then officially released in July 1980, following a rapid succession of other major events for the band. "en marzo de 1980 se graba el closer ... y en julio se lanza el álbum closer."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Rapid and Evolved Production
facts.body: *Closer* was produced at an astonishing speed, less than eight months after *Unknown Pleasures*, showcasing a significant evolution in the band's sound and approach compared to their previous work. "cómo yo y division fue capaz de trabajar un segundo al bún tan rápido estamos diciendo que no habían pasado ni ocho meses es el ano pleasure ya estaban sacando un segundo disco además muy evolucionado con respecto a su trabajo interior."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Blended Creative Periods
facts.body: Critics have often noted that *Closer* feels like two distinct albums interwoven, as it combines musical ideas and compositions already developed during the *Unknown Pleasures* era with newer material the band had been working on in the preceding months. "más que un disco closer son casi como dos discos juntos y entre mezclados porque tenemos una parte que viene como de grabaciones y de ideas y de demás ya compuestos del trabajo del primer disco la no pleasure y por otro lado tenemos las ideas que estaba trabajando la banda en esos anteriores meses."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Rapid Physical Recording, Producer-Intensive Production
facts.body: Similar to their previous album, the physical recording of the tracks for *Closer* was extremely fast, taking only a couple of days, while Martin Hannett's production work, along with the rest of the band, consumed the majority of the time and cost associated with the album's creation. "la grabación física de los temas fue muy rápida duro apenas son par de días y el trabajo de producción de Martin Hannity del resto de la banda fue el que acabó copando una gran parte del tiempo y un gran una gran parte del coste del trabajo del yoidivision."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Reflecting Live Evolution
facts.body: The album *Closer* strongly reflects the band's evolving sound observed in their early 1980 concerts, showcasing their move towards new sonic experimentation. "eso se ve muchísimo en el closer."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Experimental Sound Palette
facts.body: *Closer* features extensive musical experimentation that extends far beyond traditional guitar sounds, incorporating strong influences from synthesizers and various sound effects, contributing to an exciting and complex sonic landscape. "el closer tiene una parte ya de experimentación mucho más allá del sonido de guitarra es apasionante tenemos muchas influencias de sintetizadores tenemos muchas influencias de efectos de sonido."

facts.title: Artistic Superiority over Unknown Pleasures
facts.body: Despite internal band issues during its creation, *Closer* is considered a superior artistic achievement compared to *Unknown Pleasures*, demonstrating the band's significant progress and ambition. "el trabajo que hacen en closer es mucho mejor que el trabajo que hicieron en la nou pleasures y la banda va mucho más allá."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Balanced Sound and Simpler Lyrics
facts.body: In *Closer*, the band achieved a more balanced sound where Ian Curtis was less predominant, and his lyrics written in late 1979 and 1980 were noted as being simpler, less passionate, or less depressing, which allowed for a greater focus on the overall band sound and instrumental contributions. "aquí en el closer si que vemos un sonido mucho más de la banda Ian Cortes posiblemente no están predominantes y que es verdad que las letras que compuso Ian Cortes a final de 79 y en el 80 que formarían parte de este close up y eran un poco más vanales no eran como tan pasionales ni tan deprimentes a lo mejor son como un peline más sencillas eso permite focalizarse más en el sonido de la banda y en el sonido del disco."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Balanced Three-Pillar Approach
facts.body: *Closer* is considered a more balanced album, effectively integrating three key pillars: Ian Curtis's lyrics and vocals, the band's instrumental sound, and Martin Hannett's ambient production, resulting in a more cohesive and refined work. "posiblemente son album muchísimo más equilibrado entre es parte entre espilares que es Ian Cortes con sus letras y su voz el sonido instrumental de la banda y el sonido ambiental que hacía martin jane de la producción es un album como mucho más cerrado."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Post-Suicide Charting and International Recognition
facts.body: Released 20-30 days after Ian Curtis's death, *Closer*'s launch was amplified by the surrounding tragedy, causing it to chart in numerous territories, receive generally good reviews from nearly all magazines (unlike *Unknown Pleasures*), and gain significant popularity outside the UK, with Joy Division appearing on music magazine covers in countries like Australia and Japan during the second half of 1980. "el lanzamiento del closer ya no fue como el no pleasures fue un álbum que sí se llevó a posicionar en los charts en bastantes fue un álbum que sí fue reseñado por casi todas las revistas además con realmente buenas críticas no como increíbles pero sí con bastante buenas críticas y fue un álbum que además fuera del reino unido se hizo bastante popular tenemos portadas de revistas de música en países como australia como incluso en Japón con joydivision durante la segunda mitad de 1980."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Post-Punk Masterpiece
facts.body: For purists, *Closer* is considered the true masterpiece of post-punk, even more so than the more famous *Unknown Pleasures*. "para los más puristas aunque a no pleasures es mucho más famoso closer sí que es la verdadera obra cumple de todo el post-punk."
facts.source: Music Radar Clan
facts.episode: Especial JOY DIVISION: 3. Closer y la muerte de Ian Curtis
facts.name: Closer

facts.title: Kraftwerk Influence
facts.body: This album, Joy Division's last before Ian Curtis's death, reflected Curtis's obsession with Kraftwerk, incorporating synthesizers due to their influence. "Esa obsesión se reflejan closer, el último disco que grabaron antes de su muerte."

facts.title: Influence on Kurt Cobain (early 1980)
facts.body: A young Kurt Cobain's life was profoundly changed after he discovered New Wave music by watching The B-52s perform on *Saturday Night Live* in early 1980, illustrating the band's significant cultural impact on future musicians. "People like a young Kurt Colbaine who discovered new wave when he saw the B-52s appear on Saturday Night Live in early 1980, changed his life."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: The History of Alt-Rock: Chapter 6
facts.name: The B‐52s

facts.title: Saturday Night Live Performance (1980)
facts.body: The band's appearance on Saturday Night Live on January 26, 1980, with Terry Gar as guest host, was a pivotal and shocking moment for an 11-year-old Dave Grohl, influencing his musical aspirations. "But it was the musical guest that freaked Dave out. It was the B-52s."

facts.title: Andrew Wood's Death and STP Tribute Idea (1980)
facts.body: Andrew Wood, a member of the Seattle-based band Mother Love Bone, died of an overdose in 1980. Stone Temple Pilots had planned to dedicate their "Shangri-La Dee Da" album as a double-album tribute to him, though this elaborate concept was ultimately rejected by their record label. "This record was supposed to be a double album, something about it being a tribute to Andrew Wood of the Seattle band Mother Love Bone, who died of an overdose back in 1980."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: Scott Weiland: Part 3

facts.title: Early Signing and Trust-Based Deal (1980)
facts.body: In the fall of 1980, Mute Records, a new all-synthesizer-based label, signed Depeche Mode as one of its first acts. The initial agreement was a verbal handshake deal, not formalized in writing until 1986, demonstrating a strong trust between the band and the label. "They were one of the first people to sign into a new all synthesizer base label called mute in the fall of 1980. They struck a deal whereby all proceeds from the domestic releases would be split 50 50 with the label and the money from international sales would be split 70 30."
facts.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
facts.episode: 25 Random Facts About Depeche Mode
facts.name: Mute

facts.title: Criticism of The Babys (1980)
facts.body: In December 1980, Mellencamp, then known as John Cougar Mellencamp (after going by Johnny Cougar), told a reporter for the San Francisco Examiner that The Babys were "a bullshit band," specifically targeting their song "Every Time I Think of You." "John Melanchamp, then known as John Cougar Melanchamp, after going by Johnny Cougar, told a reporter for the San Francisco Examiner that the babies were quote, a bullshit band."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 34 - A 70s Pop Manifesto - Finding Meaning in 70s Pop
facts.name: John Mellencamp

facts.title: Self-Assessment of Own Hits (1980)
facts.body: Mellencamp considered his own 1980 hits, "This Time" and "Ain't Even Done With The Night," to be "stupid little pop records." He desired to make rock music for a specific group, feeling he and The Babys were falling short. "Melanchamp, who by the way, thought that his own hits from 1980 this time and even Della Muthanite were what he called stupid little pop records."
facts.source: For the Record - The 70s
facts.episode: Ep. 34 - A 70s Pop Manifesto - Finding Meaning in 70s Pop
